title: High Pressure in the Arms, Weak Legs / Radiofemoral Delay and a Back Murmur

blocks.text: High Pressure in the Arms, Weak Legs / Radiofemoral Delay and a Back Murmur

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-12 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease (2020; Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645) · Related AMaC: AMaC secondary hypertension station; this one tests a structural cause

The patient is a man of 27 who works as a delivery driver. A blood pressure of 168/90 was found at an insurance medical. He has headaches and cramps in his legs when he runs. Please examine his cardiovascular system.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A young hypertensive man with a delayed femoral pulse and a murmur at the back has coarctation of the aorta. The marks come from feeling both the radial and femoral pulses at the same time.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates treat the blood pressure as primary hypertension, and never feel the femorals. Pass: radiofemoral delay, arm and leg pressure difference, back murmur, bicuspid valve. Fail: essential hypertension.

rows: He is well. Take the blood pressure in both arms and feel the pulses before the chest.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; both arms' pressure; radials; brachials; femorals; face; fundi.
Feel radial and femoral together, then listen at the front and the back.
"I'm going to feel your wrist and groin pulses together, then listen over the heart and your back."
Radiofemoral delay; apex; heave; click; murmur; back; scapular bruits; carotids; lung bases; cover him.
Name the lesion, the likely valve, the complications and what treatment is used.
"He has coarctation of the aorta, probably with a bicuspid aortic valve. He needs imaging and repair, usually a stent if the anatomy is suitable."
Present in order; diagnosis; complications; imaging; stent; follow-up; thank him.
Starts without consent; presses hard on the groin; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone before palpating the femoral pulses, and keeps exposure to the minimum.
Disorganised; omits the femoral pulses, both arms' blood pressure or the back.
Measures pressure in both arms, feels radial and femoral pulses together, listens at the front and the back, then checks fundi.
Also checks the brachial pulses, listens for scapular bruits and takes a leg pressure.
Reports a diastolic murmur or heart failure that is not present.
Finds raised blood pressure in the arms, radiofemoral delay, weak femorals, an ejection click and a systolic murmur at the back.
Also finds a heaving apex, collateral vessels at the scapulae and hypertensive fundal changes.
Calls it essential hypertension or renal artery stenosis.
Coarctation of the aorta, probably with a bicuspid aortic valve.
Also separates it from renal causes, Takayasu arteritis and phaeochromocytoma, and says it may be missed in childhood.
Names left ventricular hypertrophy, aortic dissection or aneurysm, endocarditis, bicuspid valve disease and heart failure; asks for echo and CT or MR angiography.
Also names cerebral aneurysm and says routine brain imaging is not recommended in people with no symptoms.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): calls sudden severe headache or tearing chest or back pain trivial.
Says he needs repair, with catheter stenting preferred when technically feasible (otherwise surgery), treat hypertension, follow up for life, and send sudden severe pain to emergency care.

Also gives the criteria for intervention (hypertension with an invasive peak-to-peak gradient of 20 mmHg or more, or 50% or more narrowing at the diaphragm), lifelong specialist follow-up, and sport advice.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: slim and well; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure right arm 168/90, left arm 164/88, legs 110/70; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Radial pulses full; femoral pulses weak and delayed. Collateral vessels palpable around the shoulder blades. Fundi: arteriolar narrowing. Apex beat heaving, not displaced. Ejection click at the apex. Systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder at the back between the shoulder blades. No diastolic murmur. Lungs clear. No oedema.
Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Complications? (E) 4. Which tests? (E) 5. How do you treat it? (E)

Curveballs: He asks if he needs a brain scan: not routinely if there are no symptoms; sudden severe headache is an emergency. He has tearing chest and back pain: emergency, possible dissection, so immediate imaging. He wants to play football: advice from the congenital team.
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about pain (G)
Measures pressure in both arms, and in the legs (A)
Feels radial and femoral pulses together (A)
Finds radiofemoral delay, collaterals and a back murmur (B)
Finds an ejection click and heaving apex (B)
Names coarctation of the aorta with a bicuspid valve (D)
Lists dissection, aneurysm, endocarditis and left ventricular hypertrophy (E)
Requests echo and CT or MR angiography (E)
Says he needs repair, with stenting preferred when technically feasible (E)
Covers him, cleans hands and thanks him (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Sit back. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Checks one arm only.) [R2 Fail] Heart failure and a diastolic murmur. [R3 Fail] Essential hypertension. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Complications and warning signs?
CANDIDATE: Heart failure. [R5 Fail] A sudden bad headache is just stress. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): sudden severe headache or tearing chest or back pain may be a rupture or dissection. No consent, one arm only, and the cause missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Both arms' pressure, radial and femoral pulses together, front and back of the chest, fundi.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Blood pressure is high in the arms, the femoral pulses are weak and delayed, there is an ejection click and a systolic murmur at the back. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Coarctation of the aorta, probably with a bicuspid aortic valve. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Left ventricular hypertrophy, dissection or aneurysm, endocarditis, bicuspid valve disease and heart failure. Echo and CT or MR angiography. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Treatment?

CANDIDATE: He needs repair, by catheter stenting if the anatomy is suitable and otherwise surgery; I'd treat the hypertension, and he needs lifelong follow-up. Sudden severe pain goes to emergency care. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not name the differential, cerebral aneurysm advice or the invasive gradient for intervention.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine your heart? Would you like a chaperone before I feel your groin pulses? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Both arms' and leg pressure, brachials, radiofemoral together, scapular bruits, back and front; fundi.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Radiofemoral delay, collaterals at the scapulae, heaving apex, ejection click, back murmur, hypertensive fundi. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: Coarctation with a bicuspid valve, not renal hypertension, Takayasu arteritis or phaeochromocytoma; it was missed in childhood. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Left ventricular hypertrophy, dissection, aneurysm, endocarditis, cerebral aneurysm. Routine brain imaging isn't advised if asymptomatic. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Treatment?

CANDIDATE: Repair when hypertensive with an invasive peak-to-peak gradient of 20 mmHg or more, or 50% or more narrowing at the diaphragm; covered stent preferred if technically feasible; lifelong specialist follow-up; sudden severe pain is an emergency. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, leg pressure, the differential, cerebral aneurysm advice, the intervention gradient and specialist follow-up.
R2: Not feeling the femoral pulses. The delay behind the radial pulse is the diagnostic sign.
R4: Calling it essential hypertension. A young man with leg-arm differences has a structural cause.
R5: Naming hypertension alone. Dissection, aneurysm and endocarditis are the risks.
R6: Dismissing a sudden severe headache or tearing pain. Rupture or dissection can be fatal.
"May I feel the femoral pulses at the same time as the radials?"
"The arm and leg pressures differ, so I'd say coarctation."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Coarctation: hypertension in the arms with a lower leg pressure, radiofemoral delay, collaterals and a systolic murmur at the back. A bicuspid aortic valve is a frequent associated lesion in published series, with ascending aortic dilatation.

ESC 2020 (class I, level C): repair is indicated in hypertensive patients with an increased non-invasive upper-to-lower limb gradient confirmed invasively (peak-to-peak 20 mmHg or more), with stenting preferred when technically feasible; covered stents are favoured. Stenting should also be considered in hypertensive patients with 50% or more narrowing relative to the diaphragm-level aorta even if the gradient is under 20 mmHg (class IIa), and in normotensive patients with a confirmed gradient of 20 mmHg or more (class IIa); in normotensive patients with 50% or more narrowing it may be considered (class IIb). Routine imaging for cerebral aneurysm in asymptomatic patients is not recommended.
Lifelong follow-up in an adult congenital heart disease service, including surveillance of the aorta and any bicuspid valve; the interval is set by the specialist.
THINK: Young, hypertensive, weak femorals: coarctation.
SAY: "Coarctation with a bicuspid aortic valve."
DO: Both arms; radiofemoral together; the back.
NUMBERS: Repair if hypertensive with invasive gradient 20 mmHg or more, or 50% or more narrowing; stent if feasible (ESC 2020).
TRAP: Essential hypertension; missing femorals.
FINISH: Echo, CT or MRA, repair (stent if feasible); sudden pain is an emergency.

ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease (2020), key points. ACC. https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2020/08/29/13/17/2020-esc-guidelines-for-adult-chd-esc-2020 Supports: No routine cerebral aneurysm imaging in asymptomatic coarctation.

Baumgartner H, De Backer J, et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaa554 Supports: section 4.6, recommendations for intervention in coarctation and re-coarctation (full text checked): repair in hypertensive patients with an invasive gradient of 20 mmHg or more, stenting preferred when technically feasible; stenting also considered with 50% or more narrowing; routine screening for circle of Willis aneurysm not recommended in asymptomatic patients.
